results.text: FI-10 Before a wildfire: warnings, evacuation routes and supplies. FEMA's advice for preparing before a wildfire: sign up for your community's warning system. Know your community's evacuation routes, find several ways to leave the area, drive the evacuation routes and find shelter locations, and have a plan for pets and livestock. results.text: FI-04 Soot, fumes and who is most at risk. Toxicity of soot and fumes near active burning depends on what is burning, wind direction and speed, and the concentration and size of the particles. Burning plastics common in household furnishings produce highly toxic soot. People with heart or lung conditions, the elderly, smokers and children may be most affected. Evaluators of burned buildings can also be exposed to latent chemical hazards from products of combustion. Source: FEMA P-2055, Post-disaster Building Safety Evaluation Guidance (2019), PDF pages 62, 88. Origin of the sources: US. Audience: public. Type: taken from the sources. ## FI-05 Staying indoors during a smoke episode (smoke only, not approaching flames) Smoke exposure, not flame danger: during a smoke episode, a common advisory is to stay indoors, where people can better control their environment. Relief from smoke and heat is best when buildings have filtered air and climate control, and some communities provide public cleaner-air shelters for people whose buildings lack adequate filtration or cooling. In high heat, staying cool, hydrated and inside helps. Follow local emergency managers and public health officials on decisions to shelter in place. This advice concerns smoke, not approaching flames. If flames approach or the authorities order an evacuation, the evacuation order takes priority. Source: FEMA P-2055, Post-disaster Building Safety Evaluation Guidance (2019), PDF page 89. Origin of the sources: US. Audience: public.
